interactions.title: Check yourself: flow vs congestion control

questions.prompt: A capture shows the receiver advertising `window 0`. Which mechanism is acting, and where is the bottleneck?
options: Congestion control — a router is overloaded
Flow control — the receiving application is not reading fast enough
Congestion control — the sender's cwnd is 0
questions.explanation: The Window field is the receiver's advertised rwnd. Zero means its receive buffer is full because the application has not read the data — flow control. The network is not the bottleneck.

questions.prompt: rwnd = 64 KB and cwnd = 20 KB. How much unacknowledged data may the sender have in flight?
questions.explanation: The sender is limited by min(rwnd, cwnd) = 20 KB. Here congestion control, not the receiver, is the limit.

questions.prompt: During slow start, cwnd is 8 segments and every segment is acknowledged. About how big is cwnd one RTT later?
questions.explanation: In slow start cwnd grows by one segment per ACK, so it doubles every round trip: 8 → 16. Above ssthresh it would grow by about one segment per RTT instead.

questions.prompt: cwnd = 30 segments when three duplicate ACKs arrive (Reno). What happens?
options: cwnd drops to 1 and slow start restarts
Fast retransmit; ssthresh and cwnd become 15
questions.explanation: Duplicate ACKs show data is still flowing (mild congestion): the lost segment is retransmitted immediately and cwnd is halved (fast recovery). Only a retransmission timeout resets cwnd to 1.

options: The receiver tells the sender its cwnd
Routers advertise the cwnd in the IP header
cwnd is private to the sender; only rwnd travels in the TCP header
questions.explanation: The sender computes cwnd from signals such as loss, delay and ECN and never transmits it. The receiver's rwnd is in every segment's Window field. UDP has no congestion control — protocols built on it (QUIC) add their own.
